walkthrough:
**Calculate heat gained by the water**

Think like the water. It needs heat to warm up, and we can calculate it exactly.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$q = mc\Delta T$$

**Put in the numbers for water**

Temperature rise is $100 - 12 = 88^{\circ}\text{C}$. Specific heat capacity of water is $4.18 \text{ J g}^{-1} {}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$.

$$q = 250 \times 4.18 \times 88 = 91960 \text{ J} \approx 92.0 \text{ kJ}$$

**Allow for the inefficient burner**

Only 47% of the combustion heat gets to the water, the rest is lost. So total heat released must be bigger.

$$\text{total heat released} = \frac{\text{heat to water}}{0.47} = \frac{92.0}{0.47} \approx 195.7 \text{ kJ}$$

**Convert heat released to mass of butane**

One mole of butane releases $2877 \text{ kJ}$. Find moles needed, then change to mass with $M_r = 58$.

$$\text{moles} = \frac{195.7}{2877} \approx 0.0680 \text{ mol}$$
$$\text{mass} = 0.0680 \times 58 \approx 3.94 \text{ g}$$

options.A: Incorrect. $0.068 \text{ g}$ is the number of moles ($0.0680 \text{ mol}$), not the mass. You must multiply by $M_r$ of butane, $58 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, to get grams.
options.B: Incorrect. $1.85 \text{ g}$ is what you get if you forget the 47% efficiency and assume 100% heat transfer. It comes from $92.0 / 2877 \times 58$. You must divide by 0.47 because much more fuel is needed.
options.C: Correct. The water needs about $92.0 \text{ kJ}$, so total heat from combustion is $92.0 / 0.47 \approx 195.7 \text{ kJ}$. That is $195.7 / 2877 \approx 0.0680 \text{ mol}$, which is $0.0680 \times 58 \approx 3.94 \text{ g}$.
options.D: Incorrect. $4.48 \text{ g}$ comes from using $\Delta T = 100^{\circ}\text{C}$ instead of $88^{\circ}\text{C}$. The water starts at $12^{\circ}\text{C}$, so rise is $100 - 12 = 88^{\circ}\text{C}$.
